lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: So, Carian — what exactly are you so proud of? What makes you think you deserve to outrank the rest of us?
lines.note: Diogenes opens with his standard customs-officer greeting: courteous in form, contemptuous in content. 'Carian' is a pointed use of ethnicity as diminutive.

lines.speaker: Mausolus
lines.text: My kingdom, for a start, man of Sinope. I ruled all of Caria, held sway over parts of Lydia, brought several islands to heel, pushed as far as Miletus — most of Ionia under my thumb. And I was handsome. And tall. And formidable in the field. But the greatest thing — [pause] — the greatest thing is my tomb in Halicarnassus. Colossal. No other dead man has anything like it. Horses and men carved from the finest marble, portraits so exact they almost breathe — you wouldn't find a temple to rival it. Don't I have every right to be proud of all that?
lines.note: Mausolus lists his credentials with genuine relish. He saves the tomb for last, as his trump card.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Your kingdom. Your looks. And the sheer weight of your tomb.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Well, my handsome Mausolus — that strength is gone. The looks are gone. If we were to hold a beauty contest right now, I genuinely cannot tell you why your skull would be judged prettier than mine. We're both bald. Both bare. We show the same teeth, we've lost the same eyes, our noses have gone equally flat. As for your tomb and all those magnificent stones — yes, they may give the people of Halicarnassus something to show off to tourists, some grand monument they can take credit for. But you, my friend — I fail to see what good it does you personally, unless your argument is that you are better off than us because you have more weight on top of you.
lines.note: The skull-equality argument delivered as a calm anatomical survey. 'Beauty contest' is Diogenes' own framing — not mockery, just logic. The final clause ('more weight on top of you') is the line that lands.

lines.speaker: Mausolus
lines.text: All of it meaningless, then? Mausolus and Diogenes — equals? [pause] That can't be right.
lines.note: Genuine distress, not rhetorical posturing. The pause is the sound of a man who has never seriously entertained this possibility.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Not equals — no, you're right, not equals. Not at all. Mausolus will spend eternity weeping over the life above ground that he thought was so glorious. Diogenes will spend it laughing at him. And yes, Mausolus has a tomb in Halicarnassus — very impressive, built by his wife and sister Artemisia. As for Diogenes' body, whether it has a tomb somewhere — [pause] — I have no idea. Never mattered to me. But I left behind something among the finest men of my age: a reputation for a life lived higher, [pause] you most slavish of Carians, than your monument — and built on far more solid ground.
lines.note: Diogenes' closing speech is the dialogue's punchline. 'Higher than your monument' is the key line — delivered as a plain statement of fact, not a boast. 'Most slavish of Carians' is the sharpest insult in the dialogue and lands better for how long Diogenes waited to use it.
